overview.title: The promise of AI: 2017 predictions revisited in 2025
overview.main_topic: The authors' 2017 forecast of AI's impact, checked against 2025 reality, the internet-bubble analogy for coming setbacks, and the chapter's closing motto: don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision
overview.central_idea: AI's long-term trajectory resembles the internet's: a 2017 prediction that AI would become assistant, friend, interface to information and scientific collaborator has largely come true by 2025, and although a dot-com-style crash may interrupt the ride, AI will eventually be applied to nearly every process in society.
overview.importance: This page closes chapter 1 and fixes the attitude the reader is meant to carry through the book: skeptical of short-term hype (sections 1.10–1.11) but convinced of the long-term transformation. The self-check of the 2017 prediction is also the authors' evidence that the long-term vision is not itself hype.
learning_objectives: Summarize the 2017 prediction quoted on the page and list which parts the authors say have come true by 2025.
Explain the 1995/1998–1999 internet analogy and what it implies about possible setbacks for AI.
State the chapter's closing principle and relate it to sections 1.10 and 1.11.
Name the 2025 examples given for each predicted role of AI (assistant, friend, driving, science).
prerequisites: Sections 1.10–1.11 (p.36–38): the hype, the AI winters and the 2023–2025 bubble
Section 1.9 (p.35–36): the list of deep learning's achievements, several of which reappear here

summary:
The last page of chapter 1 continues section 1.12, *The promise of AI*. The author quotes what he wrote in the 2017 first edition: it may be hard to believe AI could have a large impact because it is not yet widely deployed — just as in 1995 few people could see how the internet would change their lives — but 'make no mistake: AI is coming.' The 2017 text predicted that AI would be your **assistant, even your friend**; answer questions, help educate your kids, watch over your health; deliver groceries and drive you from A to B; be your **interface to an increasingly complex, information-intensive world**; and, most importantly, help humanity move forward by **assisting scientists** in breakthroughs from genomics to mathematics.

Fast-forwarding to 2025, the authors say most of this has come true or is on the verge, and give four pieces of evidence:

- Tens of millions of people use chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude daily; question-answering and homework help ('educating your kids') turned out to be their top applications, and for many, AI is already the go-to interface to the world's information.
- Hundreds of thousands interact with AI 'friends' in applications such as Character.ai.
- Fully autonomous driving is deployed at scale in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Austin.
- AI is accelerating science: DeepMind's AlphaFold predicts protein structures with unprecedented accuracy, and Terence Tao expects that by around 2026 AI could be a reliable co-author in mathematical research when used appropriately.

The AI revolution is 'rapidly unfolding before our eyes.' There may be setbacks, as when the internet industry was overhyped in 1998–1999 and crashed, drying up investment through the early 2000s — but we will get there: AI will be applied to nearly every process in society and daily life, as the internet is today.

The chapter ends with its motto: **Don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.** It may take a while for AI to reach its true potential — the full extent of which no one has yet dared to dream — but AI is coming and will transform the world in a fantastic way.

paragraphs.excerpt: Right now, it may seem hard to believe that AI could have a large
paragraphs.what_it_says: Introduced by 'In 2017, in this very book, I wrote:', this block quote reproduces the first edition's forecast. In 2017 AI was not yet widely deployed, so its future impact was as hard to believe as the internet's was in 1995, when most people could not see how it was relevant to them. 'But make no mistake: AI is coming.' It would become your assistant and even friend; answer questions, educate your kids, watch your health; deliver groceries and drive you; be your interface to a complex, information-intensive world; and — most importantly — help humanity move forward by assisting scientists across all fields, from genomics to mathematics.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The quote serves two purposes. It is a concrete, dated prediction that can be audited (which the next paragraph does), and it establishes the internet as the authors' reference model for AI adoption: a technology whose relevance was invisible to most people shortly before it became ubiquitous. Note the ordering of the predictions — consumer roles first, then 'even more important', science.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: A prediction made eight years earlier and now checked is the authors' way of showing that the *long-term* vision, unlike the short-term hype of p.36–38, has a track record. It also shows the reader what kind of claim the authors are willing to make: broad deployment, not AGI.
connections: p.17: the preface makes the same point — AI will reach every problem where it provides utility, a transformation that will take decades.
p.38: the 'long-term picture is looking bright' sentence that opens section 1.12.

paragraphs.excerpt: Tens of millions of people are using AI chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini,
paragraphs.what_it_says: After 'Fast-forwarding to 2025, most of these things have either come true or are on the verge of coming true — and this is just the beginning', the first bullet: tens of millions of people use chatbots like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude daily as assistants; question-answering and 'educating your kids' (homework assistance) are the top applications; for many, AI is already the go-to interface to the world's information. Second bullet: hundreds of thousands of people interact with AI 'friends' in applications such as Character.ai.
paragraphs.what_it_means: These two bullets tick off the first group of 2017 predictions: assistant (chatbots), answering questions and educating kids (the top chatbot uses), interface to information (go-to source), and friend (Character.ai). The exclamation mark on 'top applications' signals the authors' own surprise that the educational use came true so literally.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: They are the evidence base for the claim that the long-term vision is sound. Note the scale words — 'tens of millions' for assistants, 'hundreds of thousands' for friends — which quietly rank how far each prediction has come.

terminology.meaning: An application in which people converse with AI 'friends' (persona chatbots); the page's example for the 'even your friend' prediction.

connections: p.36: 'Fluent and highly versatile chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini' head the achievements list in section 1.9.

paragraphs.excerpt: Fully autonomous driving is already deployed at scale in cities like Phoenix,
paragraphs.what_it_says: Third bullet: fully autonomous driving is deployed at scale in cities like Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Austin.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This checks off 'drive you from point A to point B'. The 'deployed at scale' qualifier matters: the claim is about public commercial deployment in named cities, not about research demos.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Autonomous driving was for years the standard example of over-promised AI; the authors cite it as something that has now actually shipped, which strengthens their case that the 2017 vision was realistic.
connections: p.36: the same four cities appear in the section 1.9 list: 'Human-level autonomous driving, already deployed to the public in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Austin as of 2025.'

paragraphs.excerpt: AI is making major strides toward helping accelerate science. The AlphaFold model
paragraphs.what_it_says: Fourth bullet: AI is making major strides toward accelerating science. DeepMind's AlphaFold helps biologists predict protein structures with unprecedented accuracy. Mathematician Terence Tao believes that by around 2026, AI could become a reliable co-author in mathematical research and other fields when used appropriately.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This addresses the prediction the 2017 text called 'even more important' — assisting scientists 'from genomics to mathematics'. The two examples map exactly onto the two endpoints named in 2017: AlphaFold (biology / genomics side) and Tao's forecast (mathematics side). Tao's statement is itself a forward-looking expectation, hedged with 'when used appropriately', so this bullet is partly 'on the verge of coming true' rather than fully realized.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Scientific acceleration is the application the authors care about most; it is also where the 'cognitive automation' framing of p.37 still applies — AI as a reliable *co-author*, a tool used appropriately, not an autonomous scientist.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: AlphaFold is a deep learning model that predicts a protein's 3-D structure from its amino-acid sequence; the book mentions it only as an example and does not describe its architecture.

terminology.meaning: A DeepMind model that predicts protein structures with unprecedented accuracy; the page's example of AI accelerating biology.
A renowned mathematician quoted for expecting AI to become a reliable mathematical co-author around 2026.

connections: p.36: 'assisting oncologists or radiologists', 'predicting natural disasters' — other scientific applications in section 1.9.
p.617: the author's own long-term vision for AI in chapter 19 — models that are more like programs.

paragraphs.excerpt: The AI revolution, once a distant vision, is now rapidly unfolding before our eyes.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The AI revolution is now unfolding rapidly. There may be setbacks along the way, much as the internet industry was overhyped in 1998–1999 and suffered a crash that dried up investment through the early 2000s. But we will get there eventually: AI will end up applied to nearly every process in society and daily life, much like the internet today.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This paragraph reconciles sections 1.11 and 1.12. The dot-com crash is the template: a bubble (p.38's $200B vs $30B) can burst and investment can dry up for years *without* the underlying technology failing to transform the world. The 'much like the internet is today' comparison defines the scale of the long-term claim — ubiquity, not superintelligence.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It gives the reader a precise model for what 'a mild AI winter' (p.38) might look like and why it should not shake belief in the long-term vision.

terminology.meaning: The 1998–1999 overhyping of the internet industry followed by a crash that dried up investment in the early 2000s; the authors' analogy for possible AI setbacks.

connections: p.38: the 2023–2025 AI bubble and the author's expectation that 'some air will need to be let out.'
p.621: the conclusions repeat the internet analogy — overly hyped for a few years, but a major revolution in the longer term.

paragraphs.excerpt: Don’t believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The chapter's final paragraph: don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision. It may take a while for AI to be deployed to its true potential — a potential whose full extent no one has yet dared to dream — but AI is coming and will transform the world in a fantastic way.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The sentence compresses sections 1.10–1.12 into one rule. 'Short-term hype' refers to the AGI timelines, productivity claims and the investment bubble; 'long-term vision' refers to broad, internet-like deployment. The clause 'no one has yet dared to dream' is deliberately open-ended: the authors decline to specify the ceiling, in the same way they declined on p.38 to specify a timeline.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the stance the book asks the reader to adopt as a practitioner: build real systems, judge claims on evidence, and keep working through the bubble's deflation because the destination is not in doubt.
connections: p.25: the chapter opener's goal — recognize 'the signal amid the noise' and tell world-changing developments from overhyped press releases.
p.40: chapter 2 begins the technical work with a first neural network and the mathematical building blocks.

concepts.name: Long-term vision vs. short-term hype
concepts.definition: The authors' guiding distinction: near-term claims (imminent AGI, 100× productivity, the current investment bubble) deserve skepticism, while the long-term expectation that AI will be applied to nearly every process in society deserves belief.
concepts.intuition: Treat AI like the internet in 1995: easy to dismiss day to day, impossible to overestimate over decades.
concepts.technical: Evidence for the long-term side is the 2017 prediction audit: assistant, friend, question-answering, education, driving and scientific assistance have come true or are on the verge by 2025. Evidence for the short-term side is on p.36–38 (unmet 2023 predictions, AI winters, $200B vs $30B).
concepts.significance: It is the chapter's closing principle and the mindset the book asks practitioners to carry: build real things, ignore the noise, expect setbacks, keep going.
concepts.example: The dot-com crash of the early 2000s did not prevent the internet from becoming ubiquitous.
concepts.misconception: That the two attitudes conflict. They apply to different time horizons: one can expect a bubble to deflate and still expect decades of transformation.

concepts.name: The internet analogy for AI adoption
concepts.definition: The comparison, used twice on the page, between AI now and the internet in 1995 (hard to see its relevance before deployment) and in 1998–2003 (overhyped, crashed, then transformed everything).
concepts.intuition: A technology can be simultaneously overhyped in the short run and underestimated in the long run.
concepts.technical: Phase 1 (1995 ≈ 2017): low deployment, widespread disbelief. Phase 2 (1998–1999 ≈ 2023–2025): overhyping and a bubble. Phase 3 (early 2000s): crash and investment drought. Phase 4 (today's internet ≈ AI's future): applied to nearly every process in society.
concepts.significance: It gives the authors a historical precedent in which both the skeptical and the optimistic halves of their position held at once.
concepts.example: 'Back then, most people didn't see how the internet was relevant to them and how it was going to change their lives.'
concepts.misconception: That the analogy predicts a crash for certain. The page says 'we may face a few setbacks' — the crash is a possibility the authors want readers prepared for, not a forecast.

concepts.name: AI as an accelerator of science
concepts.definition: The use of AI to assist human scientists in making discoveries, which the 2017 text called the most important of AI's future roles.
concepts.intuition: Not an artificial scientist, but a powerful co-author and instrument for human researchers.
concepts.technical: Page examples: AlphaFold (DeepMind) predicting protein structures with unprecedented accuracy; Terence Tao's expectation that by around 2026 AI could be a reliable co-author in mathematics and other fields when used appropriately.
concepts.significance: It is the application the authors rank above consumer uses, and the one they most want readers of this book to contribute to.
concepts.example: Predicting protein structures from sequence, a long-standing problem in biology.
concepts.misconception: That 'co-author' implies autonomy. Tao's hedge 'when used appropriately' and the p.37 framing both describe a tool guided by humans.

deeper.title: Scoring the 2017 prediction against the 2025 bullets
deeper.body:
The page is structured as a prediction audit. Pairing each 2017 clause with the 2025 evidence the authors give (the pairing is mine; the authors present the two lists without an explicit table):

| 2017 prediction | 2025 evidence on the page | Status per the authors |
|---|---|---|
| 'AI will be your assistant' | Tens of millions use ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude daily | Come true |
| 'answer your questions' | Question-answering is a top chatbot application | Come true |
| 'help educate your kids' | Homework assistance is a top application (!) | Come true |
| 'even your friend' | Hundreds of thousands use AI friends (Character.ai) | Come true, at smaller scale |
| 'your interface to an … information-intensive world' | 'go-to interface to the world's information' | Come true for many people |
| 'drive you from point A to point B' | Autonomous driving at scale in four cities | Come true (in those cities) |
| 'watch over your health', 'deliver your groceries' | Not mentioned in the 2025 bullets | Unaddressed on this page |
| 'assisting human scientists … genomics to mathematics' | AlphaFold; Tao's 2026 expectation | Strides made / on the verge |

The authors' own summary — 'most of these things have either come true or are on the verge' — is consistent with this scorecard: the health and grocery clauses are the ones left unverified on the page.

deeper.title: Why the dot-com crash is the right comfort, not a warning
deeper.body:
The 1998–1999 internet bubble resembles the 2023–2025 AI bubble of p.38 in shape: investment runs far ahead of revenue, fuelled by what the technology 'might soon become'. The crash that followed dried up investment for years. Yet nobody today doubts that the internet transformed every process in society.

The lesson the authors draw is therefore double-edged in a useful way: if you are an investor, the analogy warns you; if you are a practitioner learning to build these systems (the reader of this book), it reassures you — the skills remain valuable through the drought, just as web engineering did after 2001. This reading is mine, but it is what makes the sentence 'But we'll get there eventually' belong in a chapter that spends two pages on winters.

misconceptions.claim: The authors' optimism about AI's future contradicts their warnings about hype.
misconceptions.correction: The warnings concern short-term claims (AGI timelines, productivity, the investment bubble); the optimism concerns long-term deployment. The page's own motto keeps both: 'Don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.'

misconceptions.claim: The 2017 prediction was that AI would reach human-level intelligence.
misconceptions.correction: It predicted deployment roles — assistant, friend, question-answering, education, health, delivery, driving, information interface, scientific assistance — not AGI. That is why it could come true while the AGI claims of p.37 did not.

misconceptions.claim: The page claims that all of the 2017 predictions have been realized.
misconceptions.correction: It says 'most of these things have either come true or are on the verge of coming true.' The science bullet is partly a forward expectation (Tao's 'by around 2026'), and health monitoring and grocery delivery are not addressed by the 2025 bullets.

misconceptions.claim: The authors predict there will be no setbacks for AI.
misconceptions.correction: They explicitly allow for setbacks on the model of the 1998–1999 internet bubble and the early-2000s investment drought; their claim is that the long-term outcome is not in doubt.

earlier.note: Preface: deep learning is still in its early days; the transformation will take decades.
Chapter opener: learning to tell world-changing developments from overhyped press releases.
Sections 1.8–1.9: the generative-AI age and the achievement list (chatbots, autonomous driving in the same four cities).
Section 1.10: today's AI as cognitive automation — consistent with 'co-author … when used appropriately' here.
Section 1.11: AI winters and the 2023–2025 bubble; the opening of section 1.12.

later.note: Chapter 2 opens the technical part of the book: a first neural network, tensors, backpropagation and gradient descent.
Chapter 19: limitations of deep learning, the nature of intelligence, and what the future might look like.
Section 19.4.7: the author's long-term vision — models that are more like programs.
Conclusions: the hype may recede but the impact will remain; deep learning analogous to the internet.

takeaways: In 2017 the first edition predicted AI would become your assistant and friend, answer questions, educate your kids, watch your health, deliver groceries, drive you, be your interface to information, and assist scientists from genomics to mathematics.

By 2025 most of this has come true or is close: tens of millions use ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude daily (top uses: Q&A and homework help); hundreds of thousands use AI friends; autonomous driving runs at scale in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Austin; AlphaFold predicts protein structures, and Tao expects AI mathematical co-authors by around 2026.
The internet is the authors' model: hard to believe in 1995, overhyped in 1998–1999, crashed in the early 2000s, ubiquitous today.
Setbacks are possible — a crash that dries up investment — but AI will eventually be applied to nearly every process in society and daily life.
Chapter 1's closing rule: don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.
The authors decline to bound AI's potential ('no one has yet dared to dream') just as they declined to give a timeline for human-level intelligence on p.38.

questions.question: Which 2025 observation does the page offer as evidence for the 2017 prediction 'help educate your kids'?
options: Homework assistance has turned out to be one of the top applications of AI chatbots.
AI tutors have replaced teachers in several school districts.
AlphaFold is used in high-school biology classes.
Character.ai is primarily used by students.
questions.answer: Homework assistance has turned out to be one of the top applications of AI chatbots.
questions.explanation: The first bullet says question-answering and 'educating your kids' (homework assistance) are the top chatbot applications. The page makes no claims about replacing teachers, AlphaFold in classrooms, or who uses Character.ai beyond 'hundreds of thousands of people'.

questions.question: What historical episode do the authors use to describe the setbacks AI may face, and what is their conclusion about the long run?
questions.answer: The internet industry's overhyping in 1998–1999 and the crash that dried up investment throughout the early 2000s. Their conclusion: 'we'll get there eventually' — AI will be applied to nearly every process in society and daily life, much like the internet is today.
questions.explanation: The paragraph beginning 'The AI revolution, once a distant vision' makes this comparison explicitly; it links the possible mild winter of p.38 to a precedent in which the technology nonetheless prevailed.

questions.question: Which of the following is the chapter's closing principle?
options: Don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.
Believe neither the short-term hype nor the long-term vision until AGI arrives.
Short-term gains are certain; the long-term future is unknowable.
AI will transform the world within the next two years.
questions.answer: Don't believe the short-term hype, but do believe in the long-term vision.
questions.explanation: This is quoted verbatim from the final paragraph. The second option contradicts the authors' optimism; the third inverts their position (they are skeptical of the short term, confident about the long term); the fourth is exactly the kind of timeline the authors reject on p.37–38.

questions.question: Name the two scientific examples the page gives for AI accelerating science, and the field each corresponds to in the 2017 prediction.
questions.answer: AlphaFold (DeepMind), which predicts protein structures with unprecedented accuracy — corresponding to 'genomics'/biology; and Terence Tao's expectation that by around 2026 AI could be a reliable co-author in mathematical research — corresponding to 'mathematics'.
questions.explanation: The 2017 quote ends with 'across all scientific fields, from genomics to mathematics', and the fourth 2025 bullet supplies one example at each end of that range.

questions.question: Why does the author quote his own 2017 text rather than simply asserting that AI's future is bright?
questions.answer: Because a dated, specific prediction can be audited: by listing what has come true by 2025, the author shows that the long-term vision — unlike the short-term hype criticized on p.36–38 — has a track record. It also sets the scale of the claim (deployment in everyday roles and science), not AGI.
questions.explanation: The page's structure — quote, 'Fast-forwarding to 2025', evidence bullets — is an argument from verified prediction. The authors want the reader to distinguish this kind of claim from unverifiable AGI timelines.

questions.question: How does the phrase 'when used appropriately' in the Terence Tao bullet connect to the argument of section 1.10?
questions.answer: It frames AI as a tool to be used by human researchers — a reliable co-author, not an autonomous scientist — which matches section 1.10's description of today's AI as cognitive automation that enhances computers' capabilities rather than replicating human minds.
questions.explanation: Even in the page's most ambitious example (AI contributing to mathematical research), the role is assistive and conditional on proper use, consistent with the automation-vs-intelligence distinction on p.37.

questions.question: Write down one AI prediction of your own with a date, as the author did in 2017. Is it a 'short-term hype' claim or a 'long-term vision' claim by the chapter's criteria, and what evidence would let you check it later?
questions.answer: Open-ended. A good answer makes the prediction specific and auditable, classifies it by horizon and by whether it assumes new kinds of capability (autonomy) or wider deployment of existing ones, and names concrete evidence to look for.
questions.explanation: The exercise applies the page's method — dated prediction, later audit — and the chapter's distinction between hype and vision.
